source.title: Scaling and quantization of large-scale foundation model enables resource-efficient predictions in network biology
source.authors: Han Chen; Madhavan S. Venkatesh; Javier Gómez Ortega; S. Mahesh; T. Nandi; Ravi K. Madduri; Karin Pelka; C. Theodoris

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling of held-out masked-learning loss in a biological transcriptomic foundation model, extending the scaling question beyond text models.
record.gate_note: The study reports a parameter sweep for pretraining loss per token, loss per FLOP, and held-out evaluation loss (Fig. 1e–g). It also reports downstream performance by model size. The comparison of corpus diversity at equivalent data volume is recorded separately as a finding not covered by the listed versions. Quantization, embedding robustness, and in-silico deletion results do not test the scaling claims. The width-to-depth aspect ratio was optimized by evaluating models at the same parameter count, but no outcome of that comparison is reported; it is not a result row.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains Geneformer transcriptomic masked-learning models at 38M–316M parameters. It reports that held-out loss falls as a power law in parameters (Fig. 1g), which bears on V5 (power-law form in a non-text modality). It also compares zero-shot and few-shot downstream performance across Geneformer sizes, which bears on V6. The models are not language models, so V1 is not tested directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main conclusion, however, concerns quantization: 4-bit QLoRA preserves the embedding space and matches performance while using about 15% of the time and 34% of the memory for fine-tuning. The scaling result is that loss scaled as a power law with parameters, and the largest model gave the best zero-shot gene- and cell-level performance.
record.recipe_differences: This is a transcriptomic masked-learning model scaling study, not a language-model scaling study. It varies Geneformer parameter count and measures masked-learning loss; it does not reproduce the original text-model scaling procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling comparison uses 0.1 epochs and an input size of 4,096 genes per cell. The study also reports that a more diverse corpus improved pretraining loss at equivalent data volume, but does not report corresponding scaling exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger Geneformer models reached lower pretraining loss per token processed (Fig. 1e).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models are more sample-efficient per token (a Kaplan-style observation), here in transcriptomic masked learning.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal token count, a more diverse corpus subsample gave lower pretraining loss than Genecorpus-30M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Corpus diversity affects pretraining loss at fixed data volume.

record.problems: The scaling analysis is reported for one biological model family and one training duration (0.1 epochs). Individual scaling-curve values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text, and the study does not report exponents or a small-run extrapolation test.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Image and video models, repeated data, and fine-tuning or transfer scaling are not tested. Scaling in data or compute is not fitted. The parameter range is under one order of magnitude and no exponent is reported.
No quantitative predictive relationship (a fit of downstream performance against scale or loss) is reported. Fine-tuned performance is not analysed across sizes.
Methods assert 0.1 epochs is compute-optimal but report no allocation analysis.
Aspect ratios were varied at fixed parameter count, but no outcome is reported.

missing.what: Per-size held-out loss values and any fitted exponent. Only the figure is given; source data are said to accompany the paper.
Unsupported assertion that 0.1 epochs is the compute-optimal frontier, with no frontier analysis shown.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling is secondary in this paper and evidenced only qualitatively. There are five sizes spanning about 8x, there is no exponent, and all scaling runs are 0.1 epochs. The downstream size comparisons mix models trained on different corpora and for different numbers of epochs, and GF-228M used a different batch size.

versions.untested_parts: The models are transcriptomic foundation models, not language models.
The study does not report fitting power laws on small runs and using them to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget search for an optimal parameter/token allocation or trend with compute is reported.
Although aspect ratios were varied at the same parameter count for optimization, the study does not report how architecture details affected loss.
The study tests scaling with parameter count in transcriptomic masked learning; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws.
The study reports downstream task performance by model size, but does not report a quantitative predictive relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
The study does not test whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with setup or fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Geneformer GF-38M
rows.stage_stated: pretrained for 0.1 epochs for the scaling analysis
rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out evaluation loss in a parameter scaling sweep.
rows.locator: Fig. 1g; Results, “Model performance scaled as a power law with increasing parameters”
rows.note: The authors state that held-out evaluation loss scaled as a power law with increasing parameters; the individual plotted value is not given in text.
rows.check: The power law is a property of the five-model sweep in Fig. 1g, not of a single model. Read r1–r5 together. Fig. 1g's axis shows held-out loss running from about 2.65 down to about 2.35 over 38M–316M, a span of less than one order of magnitude. No exponent is stated.

rows.subject: Geneformer GF-10M
rows.stage_stated: pretrained in 2021; fine-tuned for downstream tasks
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated fine-tuned performance on four gene-level downstream tasks.

conditions.value: dosage-sensitive versus -insensitive transcription factors; NOTCH1 targets versus non-targets; bivalent versus Lys4-only-methylated promoters; long- versus short-range transcription factors

rows.baseline: Alternative approaches fine-tuned for the tasks
rows.value: Significantly improved predictions compared with alternative approaches with fine-tuning in all tasks
rows.locator: Results, “Zero-shot predictions in gene-level tasks improved with increasing model parameters”; Fig. 2b
rows.note: The text reports an aggregate result across the four tasks; it does not give individual scores here.
rows.check: This compares GF-10M with non-Geneformer baselines (SVM, RF, LR), not across model sizes. GF-10M also differs in corpus (30M cells) and input size (2,048). Relevant scale fact: few-shot GF-10M failed to train sufficiently on tasks 3 and 4.

rows.subject: Geneformer GF-104M
rows.stage_stated: few-shot learning with 100 example cells
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated few-shot performance on four gene-level downstream tasks.

conditions.value: dosage-sensitive versus -insensitive transcription factors; NOTCH1 targets versus non-targets; bivalent versus Lys4-only-methylated promoters; long- versus short-range transcription factors

rows.value: Surpassed full fine-tuning of alternative approaches in all tasks
rows.locator: Results, “Zero-shot predictions in gene-level tasks improved with increasing model parameters”; Fig. 2b
rows.note: The text reports an aggregate result across the four tasks; it does not give individual scores here.
rows.check: The baseline is wrong for scaling. The scale-relevant contrast is few-shot GF-104M succeeding on all tasks where few-shot GF-10M failed on tasks 3 and 4. GF-10M also differs in corpus and input size.

rows.subject: Geneformer GF-316M
rows.stage_stated: zero-shot learning
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated zero-shot performance on four gene-level downstream tasks.

conditions.value: dosage-sensitive versus -insensitive transcription factors; NOTCH1 targets versus non-targets; bivalent versus Lys4-only-methylated promoters; long- versus short-range transcription factors

rows.value: Surpassed fully fine-tuned alternative approaches for all tasks
rows.locator: Results, “Zero-shot predictions in gene-level tasks improved with increasing model parameters”; Fig. 2b
rows.note: The text reports an aggregate result across the four tasks; it does not give individual scores here.
rows.check: The baseline is fully fine-tuned alternatives, not smaller Geneformer models. The scale contrast is indirect: zero-shot GF-316M against few-shot GF-104M. Training also differed: GF-316M ran 1 epoch, GF-104M 3 epochs.

rows.subject: Geneformer GF-316M
rows.stage_stated: zero-shot
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated separability and classification of tissue and cell-type classes.
rows.baseline: Zero-shot embeddings of smaller Geneformer models and original data
rows.value: The largest model was the most separable by tissue and cell type and enabled more accurate predictions than the original data
rows.locator: Results, “Zero-shot predictions in cell-level tasks improved with increasing model parameters”; Fig. 3b
rows.note: The authors describe the model-size comparison in text; individual plotted values are not included.
rows.check: Only three sizes are compared (10M, 104M, 316M), and the comparison is ordinal (largest most separable), not a predictive fit.

relationships.condition: Geneformer transcriptomic masked learning, 38M–316M parameters, 0.1 epochs, input size 4,096
relationships.reason: The authors state held-out evaluation loss scaled as a power law with parameters (Fig. 1g, r1–r5). The range is under one decade and no exponent is given.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out loss reportedly scaled as a power law with parameters over less than one decade, without a reported exponent.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot and few-shot gene-level and cell-level tasks across GF-10M, GF-104M and GF-316M
relationships.reason: Larger models gave better few-shot and zero-shot gene-level results and the most separable tissue, cell-type and disease embeddings (r17–r20). Model sizes are confounded with corpus and epochs.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models improved zero-shot and few-shot gene-level performance and tissue, cell-type and disease embedding separation, although corpus and training epochs also varied.
